title: Data protection and guest privacy
siteNotes: Who the data protection contact or lead is (name and role) and how to reach them out of hours.
Which systems and messaging apps staff are allowed to use for guest and wedding details (booking system, email, any approved work messaging) and where the policy is kept.
Where paper records, wedding files and keys are locked away, and the clear-desk or shredding arrangements.
How a subject access request or other privacy request is logged, and who answers it.
How a suspected breach is reported and logged (form, phone number) and who decides whether the ICO is told.
GM to confirm the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 changes have been checked against the venue's privacy notices and request process.
legalNotes: Personal data is information about an identified or identifiable living person. UK GDPR art. 4(1). Source: https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/personal-information-what-is-it/

Special category data: race or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, trade union membership, genetic data, biometric data used to identify someone, health, sex life or sexual orientation. UK GDPR art. 9. Source: https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/lawful-basis/special-category-data/. Examples used in the slides (allergies, access needs, religion shown in dietary requests) are good-practice illustrations: health information is special category, dietary requests may reveal health or religion.

Principles (lawfulness, fairness and transparency; purpose limitation; data minimisation; accuracy; storage limitation; integrity and confidentiality; accountability). UK GDPR art. 5. The slides teach them in plain words only.

Breach reporting: notifiable breach to the ICO without undue delay and not later than 72 hours after becoming aware of it, unless it is unlikely to result in a risk to people. Individuals must be told without undue delay if there is a high risk. All breaches must be recorded. Verified against ICO guidance: https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/report-a-breach/personal-data-breach/personal-data-breaches-a-guide/

Subject access: individuals can ask for a copy of their personal data. The general time limit is one month from receipt. NOT verified live in this session; stated from knowledge of UK GDPR art. 15 and art. 12(3). The slides only say 'pass it to your manager straight away', and the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 may adjust details. Source: https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/individual-rights/right-of-access/

Personal gain or misuse: knowingly or recklessly obtaining or disclosing personal data without the controller's consent can be a criminal offence, Data Protection Act 2018 s.170. Not re-verified this session; the slides say only 'can be a criminal offence'.

Personal messaging apps and social media: ICO guidance is that organisations must have security measures that suit the risk; sharing guest details on personal accounts is not under the venue's control. This is policy and good practice rather than a quoted rule; the venue's own policy decides what is allowed (see siteNotes).
Fines and penalty amounts are deliberately not stated.

Review Oct 2026: the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 keeps the one-month response time for subject access requests but allows the clock to be paused when the controller asks the person to clarify, and confirms searches need only be reasonable and proportionate. A statutory complaints procedure for data protection complaints is required from 19 June 2026 (secondary sources and ICO summary page; not re-read in the Act). None of this changes what staff do (pass it to the manager the same day) so slides are unchanged. 72-hour ICO breach rule unchanged. The venue's privacy notice and a complaints route should be checked by the GM.

cards.title: Data protection and guest privacy
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- tell what counts as personal data
- handle guest, couple and colleague details safely
- act at once if something goes wrong

cards.title: Personal data is everywhere
cards.body:
Personal data is any information about a living person who can be identified from it. At Black Horse Beamish that is almost everything we write down about people.

We hold it so we can serve people. We look after it because it belongs to them, not to us.

items.title: Guests
items.text: Names, phone numbers, emails, booking details, car registrations

items.title: Couples
items.text: Wedding plans, guest lists, family details, budgets

cards.title: Special category data
cards.body:
Some information needs more care because it could harm someone if it got out. That includes health, race or ethnic origin, religion or belief, sexual orientation, sex life, trade union membership, political opinions, and genetic or biometric data.

Allergies, access needs and some dietary requests can reveal health or religion.

cards.title: Use it properly
cards.body:
Use personal data only for the reason we collected it, ask only for what we need, and keep it accurate.

If you need an allergy for a meal, use it for the meal. Do not pass it around for any other reason.

items.title: Need it?
items.text: Only ask for what the job needs.

items.title: Right reason
items.text: Use it for why it was given.

items.title: Right people
items.text: Share only with those who need it.

items.title: Not for ever
items.text: Dispose of it as the manager shows you.

cards.title: Phones, screens and paper
cards.body:
Most breaches are simple mistakes, not hackers: an email to the wrong person, a screen left open, a wedding file left on a table.

> Do not put guest or couple details on your personal WhatsApp or social media. Your manager will show you what we use instead.

left.title: Do
items: Lock your screen when you step away
Check the recipient before you send

right.title: Do not
items: Post or message guest details on personal accounts
Chat about guests where others can hear

cards.title: When someone asks for their data
cards.body:
Anyone can ask us what information we hold about them. This is a **subject access request**. It might be a guest, a couple or a former colleague, and it does not need special wording. It can be spoken or written.

Do not answer it, refuse it or search for it yourself. Pass it to your manager straight away, because the clock starts when we receive it.

items.title: Spot it
items.text: Someone asks what we hold on them.

items.title: Pass it on
items.text: Tell your manager the same day.

cards.title: If something goes wrong, say so at once
cards.body:
A breach is when personal data is lost, sent to the wrong person, seen by someone who should not see it, or stolen.

The business may have to tell the ICO within **72 hours** of becoming aware, so every hour counts. Nobody is in trouble for owning up quickly. Hiding it is what makes it worse.

items.label: hours the business may have to report to the ICO
minutes to wait before telling your manager

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- Personal data is anything about an identifiable person, and some types need extra care.
- Keep it off personal WhatsApp and social media; lock screens and paper away.
- Pass any request about someone's data to your manager the same day.
- Report a mistake or loss to your manager immediately. Do not wait.

cards.q: A bride's mother asks you to send the couple's guest list and dietary needs to her personal WhatsApp so she can 'sort the seating'. What do you do?
options: Send it, since she is family and is helping the couple
Send it but delete the chat afterwards so it is not kept
Do not send it; check with your manager what to do
Send only the dietary needs, as those are less private
cards.why: Do not share couple details through personal messaging or to someone you have not checked with. Your manager decides who may have what, and how.

cards.q: A former guest asks, face to face, what information we hold about her. As long as she has not put it in writing, you can ignore it.
cards.why: A request does not have to be in writing or use special words. Pass it to your manager straight away.

cards.q: You email a booking confirmation and realise a minute later it went to the wrong guest. What is the right first step?
options: Hope they delete it
Tell your manager immediately
Email them to ask them to delete it, and say nothing else
Wait to see if they reply
cards.why: This is a personal data breach. Tell your manager immediately, because the business may have a 72 hour clock to tell the ICO.

cards.q: Which TWO of these are examples of special category data?
options: A guest's room number
A guest's severe nut allergy
A guest's car registration
A colleague's religion
A guest's booking date
cards.why: Health information such as an allergy, and religion or belief, are special categories that need extra care. Room numbers, registrations and dates are personal data but not special category.

cards.q: You are called away from the front desk with a guest's booking open on screen. What should you do?
options: Lock the screen first
Leave it, you will be two minutes
Turn the monitor away
Ask the next guest to keep an eye on it
cards.why: Lock the screen every time you step away. Even a short gap lets someone see details they should not.

cards.q: A couple's wedding file is left on the bar overnight with guest names and addresses. What is this?
options: A possible breach, so tell your manager at once
Fine, as long as nobody is known to have taken it
Only a problem if the file is later found to be lost
Something to mention at next week's team meeting
cards.why: Personal data left where others can see it is a possible breach. Report it straight away.

cards.q: You may use a guest's allergy details for any purpose that seems helpful to the business.
cards.why: Use data only for the reason it was given, such as preparing a safe meal.

cards.q: A colleague asks for another colleague's home address and bank details 'to send a card'. What do you do?
options: Give the address but not the bank details, to be safe
Give both, as they are a close friend and mean well
Do not share it; suggest they ask the person or your manager
Text the details to their personal phone so it is quick
cards.why: Colleague details are personal data. Share only with those who need it, and let the manager decide.

cards.q: A guest asks you to delete the details we hold on them. Who should deal with it?
options: You, by deleting the booking there and then
Your manager, so tell them the same day
Nobody, as a venue is never allowed to delete details
The guest's family, who can sort it out for them
cards.why: Requests about someone's data go to your manager straight away. Do not refuse, delete or promise anything yourself.

cards.q: Which is the safest way to send a guest's confirmation?
options: Your personal email, as it is quick and you know it works
A photograph of the booking sheet sent to the guest
The approved system, after checking the address is right
Personal WhatsApp, as many guests already use it
cards.why: Use the approved systems and check the recipient before sending.
